name: Magnetic cupping

card.summary: Suction cups with embedded magnets, used on the face or body in the hope of boosting circulation and a firmer, brighter look.
card.note: Cupping can leave circular bruises and, rarely, burns or infections.

quick.overview:
Magnetic cupping uses suction cups that contain magnets, combining traditional cupping with a magnetic element. People use sets for body massage and, in some products, on the face for a toned, lifted look.

Practitioners of cupping describe improved circulation; reviews of cupping generally describe low-quality studies. No study of magnetic cups for appearance was found.
quick.how: Cups are placed on the skin and suction is created by hand pump or squeeze; the magnet sits in the cup. Cups are often moved or left briefly.
quick.risks: Cupping can break small capillaries and leave circular bruises, and wet or fire cupping carry higher risks of burns, scarring and infection. It may suit some people less, such as those with certain heart or blood pressure conditions, according to health ministry guidance.

lead: Magnetic cupping is a variant of cupping therapy in which the cups contain magnets. Cupping classifications list it among the types defined by what is placed inside the cup, alongside herbal, water, ozone, moxa and needle cupping [1].

Cupping creates suction on the skin. Traditional practitioners say it clears stagnation and improves circulation, while reviews describe poor study design, and the American Cancer Society states that available evidence does not support health benefits [1]. People in appearance communities use cups on the face and body hoping for a smoother, more toned look; the added magnet is claimed by sellers to add a further effect.
No studies of magnetic cups for appearance were found.

chain: Temporary blood-flow change and skin marks
angle.text: Users apply magnetic cups hoping for improved circulation and skin tone. Suction briefly pulls the skin and can leave marks that fade.

paras: Cupping is classed by technique (dry, wet, massage, flash), suction method (fire, manual, electrical) and contents; magnetic cupping is one content-based type [1].
The origins are unclear; Iranian, Greek and Roman medicine used wet cupping, Ge Hong recorded an early Chinese use, and Chinese hospitals have used it since the 1950s [1].

Cupping breaks small capillaries, leaving circular bruises that can be mistaken for injury; possible effects include scarring, burns, infections and skin darkening, and wet and fire cupping carry the greatest risk [1].
No studies found. Reviews of cupping in general report low-quality studies, with some evidence for modest relief of musculoskeletal pain and none good for acne [1].
